analysis.one_liner: Makes the 15% capital gains rate permanent and sets a $5 million estate tax exemption with lower rates for large estates.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a markup, a vote, or any action after its January 2009 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently extend the 15% capital gains tax rate that was scheduled to expire, and would rebuild the estate tax after its scheduled 2010 repeal: a $5 million-per-person exemption (indexed to inflation), lower tax rates on inherited wealth, no tax rate above double the capital gains rate even on the largest estates, and the ability of a surviving spouse to use any unused exemption of a deceased spouse. It also terminates the federal deduction for state death taxes. Most of the money goes to households with large investments and large estates.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with large capital gains keep a 15% rate on investment profits instead of returning to 20%. The wealthiest estates — those above the $5 million exemption — pay lower rates than under prior law, and estates between roughly $3.5 million and $5 million per person escape the tax entirely. Surviving spouses benefit from portability of a deceased spouse's unused exemption, a provision that also helps some widows and widowers of modest means avoid estate tax planning costs.

how_it_helps.text: Permanently keeps the reduced capital gains rate of 15% enacted in 2003, instead of letting it return to 20% when the 2003 law's sunset arrived.

Raises the estate tax exclusion to $3.75 million in 2010, rising to a permanent $5 million in 2015 and later, adjusted for inflation, shielding far more of an estate from tax than the 2009 level of $3.5 million.

Sets the estate tax rate off the capital gains rate and doubles it only above $25 million, cutting rates on the largest estates; restores the unified credit against gift tax so large gifts get the same shelter.

Lets a surviving spouse use the unused portion of a deceased spouse's $5 million exclusion, so a couple could shelter up to $10 million without trust planning — a change that also spares middle-class widows and widowers paperwork and professional fees.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through forgone revenue: every dollar of capital gains and estate tax the bill permanently forgoes must be made up by other taxes, future borrowing, or lower government spending. State governments also lose, because the bill repeals the federal deduction for state death taxes paid.

drawbacks.text: The benefit is concentrated: the capital gains cut and the estate tax changes do the most for households with large investment portfolios and estates worth millions, while the revenue cost is spread across everyone who pays federal taxes or absorbs the effects of more borrowing.
The bill repeals the deduction for state death taxes after 2009, which raises the cost for estates that owe state inheritance or estate taxes and shifts burden toward state-level taxation.
Locking in the 15% capital gains rate permanently means the preferential rate on investment income versus wages becomes permanent, a structure that favors income from wealth over income from work.
An honest supporter would acknowledge the revenue cost: the bill is a permanent tax cut with no offsetting revenue source in its text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real but narrow benefits: permanent certainty for investors and a genuinely useful portability rule for surviving spouses, plus a higher exemption that reaches some family businesses and farms. But its largest and most permanent effects are tax reductions for the top of the income and wealth distribution, paid for by forgone federal revenue with no offsets. As designed, the balance tilts heavily toward concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Harry Mitchell introduced the bill on January 14, 2009, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Seven members cosponsored the bill: six House Republicans and one House Democrat.
The action history shows no further steps — no committee markup, no committee report, no floor vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the federal Treasury kept both the scheduled capital gains rate increase and the estate tax as it stood, sparing other taxpayers from covering the forgone revenue. Wealthy households lost a chance at permanently lower taxes on investments and large inheritances.

for.name: Rep. Harry E. Mitchell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its estate tax and capital gains provisions on January 14, 2009.

for.name: Rep. Mark Kirk
for.what_they_did: Joined Mitchell in introducing the bill; the text was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Kirk.'

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 14, 2009 and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but thin — one Democrat and six Republicans out of 431 House members — and the record shows no votes or floor debate from which to measure party positions.

industries.industry: High-income investors and heirs of large estates
industries.note: The bill permanently cuts their taxes on investment gains and large inheritances. The revenue is forgone from the federal treasury, so the cost falls on other taxpayers or on government programs.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth management services
industries.note: A permanent, indexed $5 million exemption with predictable rates creates a durable market for estate planning for large estates. The bill's portability provision would reduce planning needs for ordinary couples while locking in the wealthy's tax shelter.
The bill terminates the federal deduction for state death taxes after 2009, removing a partial federal offset for estates that pay state inheritance or estate taxes.
